_note: The frame data of the fight (docs/COMBAT.md, F1). EVERY NUMBER IS AN INTEGER COUNT OF SIM STEPS, because the simulation already runs at 60 steps a second and one step is one frame — so thirty years of published fighting-game frame data can be read straight into this file without conversion. Distances are millimetres on the fight's line, also integers: no float ever decides whether a blow lands.
_reactable_note: The opponent's startups are DELIBERATELY SLOW, and this is the finding that most shapes the fight. Measured human reaction is about 265 ms, which is 16 frames. A Street Fighter jab is 4 frames — it exists to be guessed at, in a game against another person. Against one scripted opponent the player has to be able to learn the tell and answer it, which puts every attack of his in the 18-28 frame band. Street Fighter's feel at a quarter of Street Fighter's speed.
_tuning_note: This file is the whole of the fight's balance. Change a number here and nothing else. Frame advantage on hit = hitstun - (active - 1 + recovery); on block = blockstun - the same.

strike._why: The player's one blow. 8 frames to land is fast enough to feel like yours and slow enough to be beaten by his guard. On hit it leaves you +2; on block, -4, so swinging into a raised guard is punished.

swing._why: His blow. 24 frames of startup — 400 ms — is readable by a person who has seen it once, which is the whole design. It hits harder and further than yours, and it is punishable: -11 on block.

guard._why: A guard does not make you invulnerable, it makes the exchange survivable: a quarter of the damage and blockstun instead of hitstun. Holding it is not a strategy — every blocked blow still costs, and you cannot attack while it is up.

fighters._why: 45 mm a step is 2.7 m a second, close to the world's own 2.5 tiles a second, so stepping into range inside a fight feels like walking outside one.
